name: Chhath
when: Six days after Laxmi Puja of Tihar, on Kartik Shukla Shashthi (late October to mid-November)
summary: Chhath is the great sun festival of Mithila. Over four days, women fast, then stand in Janakpur's sacred ponds at sunset and again at sunrise to offer prayers and baskets of fruit and thekua to the sun. The ghats of Ganga Sagar and Dhanush Sagar glow with lamps.
body: Chhath honours Surya, the sun, and Chhathi Maiya, a mother goddess, and is the most important festival of the Maithil and Bhojpuri plains. It falls six days after the Laxmi Puja of Tihar, on the sixth day of the bright half of Kartik. Families prepare for days, cleaning houses and ponds and making offerings of fruit, sugarcane and thekua, a crisp sweet of wheat flour, jaggery and ghee.

The festival runs over four days. Devotees, mostly women, bathe and eat a single pure meal, then keep a strict fast, often without water. On the third evening they walk in procession to the ponds and rivers carrying bamboo baskets of offerings, stand waist-deep in the water and offer arghya, a prayer and water offering, to the setting sun.

The climax is the following dawn. Before first light the ghats of Janakpur fill again with families, songs and lamps, and the devotees stand in the water facing east until the sun rises. After the dawn offering the fast is broken and prasad is shared with everyone present, including visitors. A smaller Chhath is also observed in spring, in the month of Chaitra.
tips: Be at Ganga Sagar or Dhanush Sagar at least an hour before sunrise on the final morning.
Book rooms in Janakpur weeks ahead; many families return home for Chhath.
Stay on the edges of the ghats and leave space for the devotees and their offerings.
Ask before photographing women in the water, and never use a flash during the prayers.

faqs.a: Chhath falls on the sixth day of the bright half of Kartik, six days after the Laxmi Puja of Tihar, usually between late October and mid-November. The festival lasts four days, with the main offerings at sunset on the third day and sunrise on the fourth. Check current status before you travel for the exact dates each year.

Yes. Visitors are welcome to watch from the edges of the ghats and are often offered prasad, such as thekua and fruit, after the dawn prayers. Dress modestly, keep a respectful distance from devotees in the water, and follow the lead of local families. Going with a guide helps.

Thekua is a crisp, sweet biscuit made from wheat flour, jaggery and ghee, pressed into moulds and fried. It is the main offering at Chhath and is shared as prasad after the dawn prayers. Sweet shops in Janakpur sell it around the festival.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to see Chhath in Janakpur?
faqs.a: Ganga Sagar and Dhanush Sagar, the two most sacred ponds near the city centre, have the largest gatherings. Smaller ponds across the city and villages around Janakpur are quieter and more intimate. Arrive early to find a good spot without blocking devotees.

name: Vivaha Panchami
when: Fifth day of the bright half of Mangsir (late November to mid-December)
summary: Vivaha Panchami celebrates the wedding of Rama and Sita, believed to have taken place in Janakpur. Pilgrims arrive from India with a wedding procession, and the city re-enacts the ceremony at the Janaki Mandir and Vivah Mandap over several days of music, prayer and crowds.
body: Vivaha Panchami falls on the fifth day of the bright half of the month of Mangsir, usually in late November or early December. It marks the wedding of Rama and Sita described in the Ramayana, which Hindus believe took place in Janakpur, King Janaka's capital. For Janakpur it is the biggest event of the year.

In the days before the festival, a ceremonial wedding procession, the Ram baraat, arrives with pilgrims, many from Ayodhya in India, Rama's city. Janakpur receives it as the bride's family would, with music, flowers and feasting. The Janaki Mandir and the Vivah Mandap are decorated with lights, and devotional singing goes on late into the night.

On the day itself, priests perform the wedding rituals for the images of Rama and Sita at the Vivah Mandap, following Maithil wedding customs. Pilgrims crowd the temple courtyard and streets, many dressed as for a family wedding. It is joyful, loud and very crowded, and a rare chance to see Maithil wedding traditions performed on a city-wide scale.
tips: Book Janakpur hotels well ahead; rooms fill with pilgrims from Nepal and India.
Visit the Janaki Mandir early in the morning during the festival week, before crowds peak.
Keep valuables secure and agree a meeting point with your group in the crowds.
Ask your guide to explain the Maithil wedding rituals as they happen.

faqs.a: Vivaha Panchami falls on the fifth day of the bright half of Mangsir in the Nepali calendar, usually in late November or early to mid-December. Celebrations in Janakpur run for several days before the main day. Check current status before you travel for the exact date each year.

faqs.q: What happens at Vivaha Panchami in Janakpur?
faqs.a: A wedding procession of pilgrims arrives, many from Ayodhya, and Janakpur re-enacts the wedding of Rama and Sita at the Janaki Mandir and Vivah Mandap, with Maithil wedding rituals, music, decorations and large crowds of pilgrims. The temple is lit up and devotional singing continues late into the night.

faqs.q: Is Vivaha Panchami a good time to visit Janakpur?
faqs.a: Yes, if you enjoy festivals and do not mind crowds. The city is at its most colourful and devotional. Hotels are full and prices higher, so book early. If you prefer a quiet visit, come a week or two before or after the festival.

faqs.q: Why is Vivaha Panchami celebrated in Janakpur?
faqs.a: Hindus believe Janakpur was the capital of King Janaka, Sita's father, and the place where Rama married Sita after breaking Shiva's bow. Vivaha Panchami marks the anniversary of that wedding, so Janakpur and the Vivah Mandap are its natural centre.

name: Maghi, the Tharu new year
when: Magh 1, the day of Maghe Sankranti (usually 14 or 15 January)
summary: Maghi is the Tharu new year, celebrated on the first day of Magh in mid-January. Tharu families bathe at dawn, visit relatives, eat dhikri, sweet potatoes and meat, and dance late into the night. In Chitwan's Tharu villages it is the warmest week of the winter.
body: Across Nepal, the first day of Magh is Maghe Sankranti, when the sun moves into Capricorn and the coldest month ends. For the Tharu people of the Terai it is also Maghi, their new year and their biggest festival. The day falls on a fixed date in the solar calendar, usually 14 or 15 January.

Families begin with an early bath in a river or pond, then gather at home. Younger people seek blessings from elders, and married daughters visit their parents. Food is central: dhikri, steamed rice-flour cakes, are made in large batches, along with sweet potato, tarul yam, and meat or fish curries. Rice beer is shared in many homes.

In the western Terai, Maghi is also when village affairs are settled for the coming year, and communities choose or confirm village leaders. In Chitwan's Tharu villages around Sauraha, Barauli and Amaltari, the festival brings dancing, singing and visits between houses over several days. Visitors staying in Tharu homestays are often invited to share the food.
tips: Stay in a Tharu homestay in Barauli or Amaltari to be part of the celebrations.
Try dhikri with pickle and curry; it is made fresh for Maghi.
Combine Maghi with the Maghe Sankranti mela at Devghat, held on the same day.
Pack warm layers; mid-January mornings in Chitwan are cold and foggy.

faqs.a: Maghi falls on the first day of the month of Magh in the Nepali calendar, the same day as Maghe Sankranti, usually 14 or 15 January. Celebrations in Tharu villages often continue for several days. Check current status before you travel for the exact date each year.

faqs.q: How do the Tharu celebrate Maghi?
faqs.a: With an early ritual bath, family gatherings, blessings from elders, feasts of dhikri, sweet potato, yam and meat curries, and singing and dancing. In the western Terai it is also a time for choosing village leaders and settling community affairs for the year ahead.

faqs.q: Can visitors join Maghi celebrations in Chitwan?
faqs.a: Yes, especially if you stay in a Tharu community homestay in Barauli or Amaltari, where hosts often invite guests to share the food and dances. In Sauraha, ask your lodge or a Tharu guide about village events. Always ask before photographing people and rituals.

faqs.q: Is Maghi the same as Maghe Sankranti?
faqs.a: They fall on the same day. Maghe Sankranti is observed by Hindus across Nepal with river baths and warming foods. For the Tharu, the day is Maghi, their new year and most important festival, with its own customs, foods and dances.
